title: Keeping it from breaking: check, alert, and leave a trail
promise: You'll know how to add three pieces to any automation. The first: a check on the data coming in. The second: an alert that buzzes your phone when something fails. The third: a sheet where every run gets logged. And you'll leave them tested: you'll break them on purpose, before a client breaks them for you.
why: Rocío roasts coffee in Valencia and sells bags through her website. She built a flow: a chain of automatic steps. With every order, the flow logs the row in a spreadsheet and sends the packing slip to the warehouse. One Tuesday at 3:14 AM, an order came in with an empty phone field. The box that writes to the sheet choked. The flow stopped dead. Nobody got an alert, because there wasn't one. The website kept charging cards. Not a single order reached the warehouse for nine days. She found out from an angry customer. Rescuing those 47 orders by hand cost her a whole Saturday and $400 in rush shipping.

theory.title: The silent failure costs a hundred times more than the loud one
theory.text: When you do things by hand, failures announce themselves: you're right there, you see the red screen, and you fix it on the spot. Not an automation. It works while you sleep, while you eat, and while you're with your daughter at the park. When it breaks, nobody's watching. There are two clocks here: the clock of the breakdown (3:14 AM) and the clock of you finding out (nine days later). The one that matters is the second one. Everything that fits between those two clocks is what's going to cost you money. And yes, both n8n and Make mark a failed execution in red. An execution is each complete run of the flow, start to finish. But that red lives in a list you'd have to open every day, and you're not going to open it. An alert you have to go find isn't an alert: it's a report. Worse still is the case where the flow doesn't stop: it keeps running happily along, writing crooked data. You don't find that out in nine days, you find it out in three months, when someone tries to use that sheet for something.
theory.analogy: A smoke detector at home isn't useful because it detects smoke. It's useful because it beeps. A detector that writes the smoke down in a notebook kept in the attic is an expensive decoration.
theory.example: If a message had reached Rocío's phone at 3:14 AM, she'd have seen it at 8:30 with her coffee. Filling in the phone by hand and hitting retry is four minutes. The difference between four minutes and a Saturday plus $400 isn't in the failure. It's in the alert.

theory.title: Three pieces: the doorman, the alarm, and the notebook
theory.text: Everything needed to keep an automation from giving you a bad time fits into three pieces. Each one answers a different question. The doorman (validation: checking the data as it comes in) answers "is trash getting in on me?" The alarm (the alert) answers "am I going to find out?" The notebook (the log: the list of what the flow did every time) answers "tomorrow, will I be able to reconstruct what happened?" None of them replaces the others. If you validate but don't alert, your flow will be rejecting good orders and you won't know. If you alert but don't log, you'll get an "something failed at 3:14" with no way to know with what data. If you log but don't alert, you'll have a perfect diary nobody reads. The doubt that'll come up is whether you need to build all three from day one. The answer is no: there's an order. First the alarm, which takes ten minutes and covers everything else. Then the notebook, which is five minutes and a spreadsheet. The doorman last. To write its rules you need to have seen what really comes in, and that's what the notebook tells you.
theory.analogy: A restaurant has three things. Someone who checks the goods when they come off the truck. The extractor hood alarm that goes off when something's burning. And the delivery log. Remove any of the three and the place runs exactly the same. Until the day it doesn't.
theory.example: In Rocío's case all three pieces were needed and none was there. The doorman: empty phone, stop before writing. The alarm: a Telegram message at 3:14 AM. The notebook: a row saying "order 1182, empty phone, not sent to the warehouse."

theory.title: Validating on the way in: five questions and a review tray
theory.text: Validating means asking five questions of every piece of data coming in. All five are deliberately dumb. Is the field there? Does it come in empty? Is it what I expect: a number, a date, a text? Does it have the right shape? For example, an email with an @ and a dot after it, or a nine-digit US phone number. Is it within a range that makes sense? For example, an amount between $0.01 and $500, or a delivery date that isn't last week. What matters isn't which questions, it's where. The check goes in the very first box, before anything that can't be undone. Charging a card, emailing a client, deleting a row, and publishing something don't undo. Validating after that is like checking ID after the guy's already driven off with the car. The immediate doubt is "what if I reject a good order over something silly?" The answer: the doorman never throws anything away, it sets it aside. What fails the check goes into a tab called "Review" and triggers an alert. You look, fix the phone by hand, and send it back into the flow. And one warning that'll save you scares. The AI building your flow isn't going to add any of this unless you explicitly ask for it. It builds you the happy path: the one with perfect data, which almost never arrives.
theory.analogy: Airport baggage screening. Nobody throws your suitcase in the trash because you're carrying a 5-ounce lotion. They set it aside, page you, and you sort it out in two minutes. Setting aside and throwing away aren't the same thing.
theory.example: Rocío's rules, written in one afternoon. Email with an @ and a dot after it. Phone with 10 digits. Zip code with 5 digits. Amount between $0.01 and $500. Address with at least 10 characters. Order 1182 failed the second rule. It went to "Review" and the warehouse never saw it broken.

theory.title: Alerting: it has to buzz, make sense, and not wear you out
theory.text: An alert is worth exactly where it lands. Email doesn't interrupt anyone: it sits in an inbox with forty others and you read it Thursday. Telegram, WhatsApp, or Slack do interrupt, because they buzz in your pocket. And the alert needs to carry five things or it's worthless. One: which flow broke. Two: when, with time and timezone. Three: with what specific data; the order number, not "a record." Four: what the error said, copied verbatim. Five: what you need to do now. The downside is real and it's called alarm fatigue. If it buzzes you thirty times a day, you mute it within two weeks and you're back at square one. So group repeated alerts into one per hour. And don't alert about things that don't need you to lift a finger. And there's the trickiest problem of all left. "I haven't gotten any alerts" means either everything's fine, or the alert system itself has crashed. And from the outside they look identical. That's fixed with a heartbeat. A heartbeat is a short message that reaches you every day at 9 PM. It says, for example: "today 14 runs, 13 good, 1 set aside." Once you have a heartbeat, silence stops being ambiguous: either the summary arrives, or something's wrong.
theory.analogy: A car alarm that goes off every time a motorcycle drives by. At first you check. Three weeks later nobody looks anymore, and the day someone actually tries to break in, the alarm goes off for nothing.
theory.example: Useless alert: "Error in workflow Orders." Useful alert: "ORDERS · 3:14 AM Eastern · order 1182, marta.g***@gmail.com · the phone field arrived empty · was NOT sent to the warehouse · it's in the Review tab of the Orders sheet · fill in the phone and press Retry." Both show up on the lock screen; only one tells you what to do.

theory.title: The notebook: a dead-boring sheet that saves your month someday
theory.text: The log is just another tab in your spreadsheet, called "Log." It has seven columns. Date and time with timezone. Flow name. Execution number. Reference for what came in (order 1182). Result (good / error / set aside). The literal message if it failed. And how long it took. A row gets written every time the flow completes a run, whether it goes well or badly. That's the part people skip. If you only log the errors, you can't tell whether today had zero failures or zero orders. The real value shows up when a client writes "my order from the 4th hasn't arrived." With a log, you search it and know in thirty seconds whether it came in, whether it got set aside, and why. Without a log, your answer is a shrug. Two important warnings. The first is legal and serious: never copy passwords, card numbers, full IDs, or a client's complete personal data into it. A sheet shared with three people isn't a secure place. And data protection regulations apply just as much to your two-employee shop as to a bank. Write "marta.g***@gmail.com" or just the order number outright. The second is practical: keep 90 days and delete anything older. A sheet past a few tens of thousands of rows starts dragging. And there's an unexpected reward: the log is the only thing that lets you answer "how many times has this happened?" That's the question that decides whether it's worth fixing or not.
theory.analogy: A ship's logbook. It gets filled in every day, nobody reads it, and it looks like a waste of time. Until the day you have to explain exactly what happened and at what time.
theory.example: Rocío's log showed that, out of 340 orders in a month, six came in with an empty phone. All six came from the mobile view of the form, where the field wasn't marked required. Four minutes fixing the form solved more than any patch inside the flow.

theory.title: Break it yourself on a Tuesday afternoon, not a Sunday at 3 AM
theory.text: You can't trust a net you've never fallen into. The most common failure of all isn't the flow breaking: it's the alert breaking. And that never gets discovered the easy way, because while everything's fine the alarm doesn't have to sound. So trigger it: four tests, fifteen minutes, at a time you can clean up the mess. Send an order with a required field empty, another with an email missing the @, another with an absurd amount like $9,999. Then change one letter in a service's access key, so it throws a credentials error. For each test, write down three things: what happened, whether the alert arrived, and how long it took. Watch out with the fourth test: write down the original key before touching it. Many services won't show it to you again, and you'd have to generate a new one and change it everywhere it's used. And there's a decision worth making here, not at 3 AM. Automatic retries. Retrying is free when repeating the action does no harm: rereading a sheet, rechecking a price. And it's extremely dangerous when it does: a retry on a $34.90 charge charges it twice. A retry on an email to a client sends the same notice three times. Simple rule: automatic retry only on things that can be repeated with no consequences. On anything that moves money or talks to a client, you press the retry yourself.
theory.analogy: The school fire drill. It's not done because there's a fire. It's done to discover, calmly and with no smoke, that the emergency door is locked with a padlock nobody knows who owns.
theory.example: In her Tuesday test, nothing reached Rocío's phone. She'd pasted the Telegram chat ID wrong: there was an extra trailing space. She found it out in a five-o'clock test, not with 47 orders piled up and a customer on the phone.

tasks.title: List everything that could go wrong, before touching anything
tasks.where: In the Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini app, in the chat with your automation
tasks.action: Describe your flow box by box, with the real names you gave each one. Don't ask it to fix anything yet: today you just want the list of possible breakdowns. Copy the prompt below and swap the flow description for your own. The more specific you are with sheet names, services, and field names, the more useful the list.
tasks.prompt:
I have this automation built and want to know where it can break. Do NOT modify it yet, don't give me solutions: today I just want the inventory of failure modes.

MY FLOW, BOX BY BOX:
1. [Example: an order comes in from the website's form, with these fields: name, email, phone, address, zip code, amount]
2. [Example: a row is added to the Google Sheet called "Orders"]
3. [Example: an email is sent to the warehouse with the order's details]
4. [Example: a confirmation email is sent to the client]

IT RUNS: [Example: every time someone buys, any time of day, about 12 times a day]
WHO WATCHES IT: nobody, that's why we're here.

Give me a table with these columns: WHAT CAN FAIL | IN WHICH BOX | HOW I'D FIND OUT TODAY (if I do at all) | WHAT HAPPENS IF I DON'T FIND OUT WITHIN A WEEK | SEVERITY from 1 to 5.

Include these families no matter what, even if they seem unlikely:
- data that arrives empty, misspelled, or with a line break inside
- data that arrives with an absurd value (negative amount, year-1900 date)
- the destination service down or slow
- the access key expired, revoked, or with changed permissions
- someone renaming or moving the spreadsheet
- the same order coming in twice
- the flow stopping halfway and leaving the work half done

Sort from highest to lowest severity and star the three I should fix first.
tasks.expect: A table with twelve to fifteen rows, not five. At least three or four will surprise you. "Someone renames the sheet" and "the flow stops halfway" are almost never thought through. Save that table, it's the shopping list for the rest of the lesson.
tasks.stuck: If it gives you five generic failures like "there could be a connection error," you described the flow in two vague lines. Rewrite it with real names: "the sheet is called Orders 2026," "the service is Gmail," "the field is called customer_phone." The list's quality depends entirely on that specificity.

tasks.title: Write the doorman's rules, field by field
tasks.where: In the AI app, in the same chat as the previous task
tasks.action: Now you drill down into the data. List the fields entering your flow with their exact names and paste the prompt. It'll give you back a rules table and, below it, the specific setup to paste into your tool. Don't accept rules you don't understand: the prompt's second part is there for that.
tasks.prompt:
Let's put a data check at the start of my flow, before anything gets written and before any email gets sent.

FIELDS COMING IN:
- name [text]
- email [text]
- phone [text]
- address [text]
- zip_code [text]
- amount [number, in dollars]
[swap for yours, with the exact names they have in the flow]

CONTEXT: it's a US online store, orders usually between $8 and $120, individual customers.

Give me a table: FIELD | REQUIRED? | TYPE | EXACT SHAPE I ACCEPT | REASONABLE RANGE | WHAT I DO IF IT FAILS (stop / set aside in the Review tab / continue with a default value).

Then, and this is the important part:
1. Explain EACH rule in one plain-English sentence, no jargon.
2. For each rule, give me three examples that pass and three that don't.
3. Tell me which tool to put it in and exactly what to write in each field. I use [n8n / Make / Zapier]. Tell me the node or module name, the tab, and the literal condition text.
4. Mark which of these checks absolutely MUST happen before charging a card, before emailing the client, and before deleting anything.

Non-negotiable rule: nothing gets discarded. Whatever fails the check gets set aside and alerted.
tasks.expect: A table where for each field you know what's accepted and what isn't, with instructions below giving tab and field names. If it gives you those odd symbol-heavy lines to validate emails, you need to be able to read the plain-English sentence next to it about what it accepts.
tasks.stuck: If it throws symbols with no explanation, reply: "I don't understand the email rule, explain it to me like I'm twelve and give me five emails that pass and five that don't." If it suggests rejecting and discarding instead of setting aside, cut it off: "I don't want to lose a single order, I want them set aside in a Review tab."

tasks.title: Turn on the error branch in your automation
tasks.where: In n8n or Make, in your browser
tasks.action: By default, when a box fails, the whole flow stops dead and silently. You're going to change that so the failure exits through a side door you can hang an alert off of. In n8n: click the box that can fail (the one writing to the sheet, for example) and a panel opens. At the top you'll see the "Parameters" and "Settings" tabs. Go into "Settings," find the "On Error" list, and change it from "Stop Workflow" to "Continue (using error output)." Closing the panel, you'll see a second output has appeared on the box, in red, on the right side. Drag from that red output to an empty spot: that's where you'll hang the alert in the next task. In Make: right-click the module, choose "Add error handler," and pick "Resume" so the flow continues. Repeat on the two or three most fragile boxes: the ones talking to an outside service.
tasks.expect: You see a second arrow coming out of the box, red or marked as error, different from the normal one. The canvas now has two paths: the all-good one and the something-went-wrong one.
tasks.stuck: If you can't find "Settings," you're still on the "Parameters" tab. The tabs are at the top of the panel that opened, not in the side menu. If your tool doesn't have a per-box error branch, there's another route. Open the flow menu (three dots top right), go into "Settings," and look for "Error Workflow." It's a separate flow that fires whenever anything blows up, and it works just as well.

tasks.title: Connect the alert to something that buzzes
tasks.where: In the phone's Telegram app, then in n8n or Make
tasks.action: You're going to create a Telegram bot: an automatic account that sends you messages. It's free and takes three minutes. In Telegram, search for @BotFather (the one with the verified badge), open it, press "Start," and type /newbot. It'll ask for a display name ("Order Alerts") and then a username that has to end in bot ("rocio_alerts_bot"). It'll give you back a token: a long string of letters and numbers that works like a password. Save it in your password manager. Never paste it into a public chat or let it show up in a screenshot. Now find your newly created bot, open it, and press "Start": if you don't, the bot can't message you. To find out which chat to send messages to, search @userinfobot, press "Start," and it'll give you your ID number. Go back to n8n and drag a Telegram box onto the end of the red branch. Create a new credential by pasting the token. Put your number in "Chat ID" and type any test text. Press "Test step."
tasks.expect: Your phone buzzes within five seconds with the test message. If it buzzes, you've now built the piece Rocío was missing.
tasks.stuck: Getting "chat not found"? Two possible causes. Either the number is copied wrong, or you didn't press "Start" on your bot. Check no space snuck in at the end. Press "Start" and try again. If Telegram feels like a hassle, a Slack message or an email works just as well. Just make sure to enable that email's notification on your phone. What doesn't work is one more email among forty others.

tasks.title: Write the alert message that actually makes sense at 3 AM
tasks.where: In the AI app, then copying the result into the Telegram box
tasks.action: The alert's wording matters more than it seems: you're going to read it half-asleep on the lock screen. Ask for it with the prompt below. Paste the result into the Telegram box's "Text" field. Replace the placeholders with your flow's real data; in n8n they get dragged in from the left panel.
tasks.prompt:
Write me the template for the alert message I'll get on my phone when my automation fails.

CONTEXT: I'm [Rocío, online coffee shop]. The flow is called [ORDERS]. Typical failures are: required field empty, misspelled email, the spreadsheet not responding, the service's key expired.

THE MESSAGE HAS TO FIT ON THE LOCK SCREEN AND CARRY EXACTLY THIS:
1. First line: which flow and what broke, in five words.
2. When, with time and saying the timezone.
3. With what specific data: order number and email with the middle part masked with asterisks. No full personal data.
4. The error message copied verbatim, even if it's in English... it already is.
5. What did NOT happen because of the failure (for example: "the warehouse wasn't notified").
6. Last line: what I need to do, as a single instruction.

7 LINES MAX. No greeting, no "dear user," no decorative emojis (one at the start to tell error from alert at a glance is fine).

Give me the template with placeholders marked like this: {{order_number}}, {{time}}, {{error_message}}. And below it, write three already-filled-in examples: one for an empty field, one for a service being down, and one for an expired key, so I can see how they really look.
tasks.expect: A six- or seven-line template that reads in one pass. The first line says what broke and the last says what you do. The three filled-in examples let you see whether it really makes sense.
tasks.stuck: If it gives you a fifteen-line wall of text, reply: "too long, 6 lines max, the first says what broke and the last what I do, cut everything else." If it includes the client's full email or phone, tell it to mask them with asterisks. That message is going to sit in your Telegram history forever.

tasks.title: Create the log sheet and the box that logs every run
tasks.where: In Google Sheets, and then in your automation
tasks.action: Open the spreadsheet your flow already uses and create a new tab at the bottom, with the + sign, called "Log." In the first row write these seven headers, one per column: datetime, flow, execution, reference, result, message, seconds. Go back to your automation. Add a Google Sheets box with the "Append Row" action at the END of both branches: the good one and the red one. On the good one, the result will be "good"; on the red one, "error." Use the prompt to find out what to drag into each column.
tasks.prompt:
I have a tab called "Log" in Google Sheets with these exact columns: datetime, flow, execution, reference, result, message, seconds.

I want to write a row every time my flow completes a run, whether it goes well or badly. I use [n8n / Make / Zapier].

Tell me, column by column, what value to put in and where to get it from within the tool (the exact name of the data or variable I need to drag or type). Keep in mind:
- datetime has to show US Eastern time, not universal time. Tell me exactly how to configure that, because I know it defaults to a few hours off.
- reference: the order number, never the client's name or address.
- result: only three possible values, "good," "error," or "set aside."
- message: empty if it went well; the literal error if it failed, trimmed to 200 characters.

Then answer three things for me:
1. Which of my fields should I NEVER write here for data protection reasons, knowing three people on my team see this sheet.
2. How I automatically delete rows older than 90 days, or whether it's better for me to do it by hand once a month.
3. What formula to put in a separate cell to see at a glance how many errors I have today.
tasks.expect: You run the flow once and a new row shows up in "Log" with the correct time and result "good." Trigger a failure and another shows up with result "error" and the message next to it.
tasks.stuck: If the time is off by one or two hours, it's writing in universal time. In n8n it's changed in the flow menu: "Settings" then "Timezone," picking your local zone. If the row's columns come out shuffled, check the sheet's headers. They have to be written exactly like in the box, no extra capitals or stray spaces.

tasks.title: Set up the daily heartbeat so silence means something
tasks.where: In n8n or Make, in a new flow separate from the main one
tasks.action: Create a new flow and name it "Heartbeat." The first box is a "Schedule Trigger": set it to 9:00 PM, every day. The second reads your sheet's "Log" tab. The third counts today's rows and splits them by the result column. The fourth sends you a one-line Telegram message: "ORDERS · today 14 runs · 13 good · 1 set aside · 0 errors." That message has to reach you on the days everything's perfect too: that's exactly the point. From now on, if nothing's arrived by 9:15, you know to check.
tasks.expect: At 9:00 PM your phone buzzes with a one-line summary. The next day, another one. Once you've received it three days in a row, your brain will already be expecting it and you'll notice its absence.
tasks.stuck: If it arrives at an odd hour, the flow's timezone isn't yours: flow menu, "Settings," "Timezone," pick your local zone. If setting up the count feels like too much, start with a dumb version that just says "ORDERS still alive" at 9:00 PM. It covers 80% of the purpose and takes four minutes to build.

tasks.title: Break it on purpose with four poisoned inputs
tasks.where: In your flow's form or real input, at a time you can clean up the mess
tasks.action: Generate four bad inputs with the prompt and send them one at a time through the same channel real data comes in through. After each one, write down three things on paper: what happened, whether the alert arrived, and how long it took. Do it on a Tuesday afternoon, never a Friday at eight.
tasks.prompt:
Generate four test inputs to deliberately break my flow, each in a different way.

MY FLOW RECEIVES THESE FIELDS: [name, email, phone, address, zip_code, amount]
NORMAL VALUES: [amounts between $8 and $120, US customers]

I WANT FOUR TESTS:
1. A required field arriving empty.
2. A field with the wrong shape (an email missing the @).
3. A value out of range that looks legitimate but isn't (an amount of $9,999).
4. A value with characters that tend to break things: quotes, a line break inside the text, an accented character, an emoji, and 500 characters of length in the address field.

For EACH one give me, as a table: THE EXACT DATA I SEND | WHAT SHOULD HAPPEN IF MY PROTECTION WORKS | WHAT WILL HAPPEN IF I DON'T HAVE IT | HOW I CHECK IN 30 SECONDS WHICH OF THE TWO HAPPENED.

Also warn me which of these four tests could leave something half-done that I'd have to clean up by hand (a junk row, an email sent to a fake client), and tell me how to clean it up.
tasks.expect: All four fail in a controlled way. Nothing gets written into the good sheet. All four show up in "Review" or the log with result "error." And you get four alerts on your phone. Four of four, not three.
tasks.stuck: If the flow stops completely and nothing arrives, the error branch isn't connected to the alert: go back to task 3. Does the bad input sail through and write the row? Then the check is placed after the writing box. Move it to the very first position. If it left junk in the sheet, delete it right now. See it tomorrow and you'll think it's a real order.

tasks.title: Break a key on purpose to check whether the alarm sounds
tasks.where: In n8n or Make, on the credentials screen
tasks.action: This is the test almost nobody runs, and the one that catches the most failures. FIRST: copy the current key and save it in your password manager. Many services won't show it to you again. If you lose it, you'll have to generate a new one and change it everywhere it's used. Now go into the credential one of your boxes uses. Change one single letter at the end, save, and run the flow by hand with the "Execute Workflow" button. When you're done testing, put the good key back and run it again. That confirms everything's back to normal. If touching the production flow — the one working for real with your clients — makes you nervous, do it on a copy instead. Three-dot menu, "Duplicate."
tasks.expect: The flow fails, and a 401, a 403, or the word "Unauthorized" shows up in the alert on your phone. That message is exactly what you'd see on a Sunday, and now you already know what it means and what to do.
tasks.stuck: If no alert arrives, that box doesn't have the error branch active: go back to task 3. Do this on the boxes using credentials too, since those are the ones that expire most. If you lost the good key, don't panic: go into the service, generate a new one, and update the credential. Then check which other flows the old one was used in, because those have stopped working.

tasks.title: Write the cheat sheet for what to do when the alarm sounds
tasks.where: In the AI app, and the result into a document next to your project
tasks.action: The last step is the one that turns all this into something that survives you going on vacation. One page, five failure modes, what to do for each. Paste the prompt with the list from task 1. Save the result in a document called "When the Alarm Sounds," in the same folder as the rest of the project.
tasks.prompt:
Write me a one-page cheat sheet titled "When the Alarm Sounds," to keep handy for when my automation alerts about a failure.

MY FLOW: [paste the box-by-box description here]
THE MOST LIKELY FAILURES ACCORDING TO MY INVENTORY: [paste the first five rows of the failure table here]
WHERE ALERTS ARRIVE: Telegram, on my phone.
WHERE THE LOG IS: "Log" tab of the Google Sheet called [Orders].

FOR EACH OF THE FIVE FAILURES, give me:
1. How I recognize it: the exact phrase I'll see in the alert.
2. Whether it's urgent right now or can wait until tomorrow morning. Be blunt, I want a yes or no.
3. The steps to fix it, numbered, with button and tab names. Five steps max.
4. What I must NOT do under any circumstances (for example: rerunning something that already charged a card).
5. How I check it's actually been fixed.

Write it for someone who doesn't code and who'll read it in a rush and in a bad mood. Short sentences. No theory. And add a line at the end with: who I call if this gets out of hand, leaving a blank for me to fill in the name.
tasks.expect: A page you could hand to someone else on your team today and they'd know how to react without calling you. If reading it yourself leaves you unsure which button to press, it's not finished yet.
tasks.stuck: If it comes out generic and full of "check the system logs," you didn't paste it task 1's inventory. Paste the whole thing and add: "I want steps with real button names, not advice." And test the cheat sheet for real. Next time an alert sounds, open it and follow it to the letter instead of improvising. That's where the gaps show up.

matters: Putting the check BEFORE anything that can't be undone. Charging a card, emailing a client, deleting a row, and publishing don't undo. Validate afterward and you've already charged $34.90 for an order with an empty address. And now you have to refund it, apologize, and pay for two shipments.

Getting the alert to land somewhere that buzzes in your pocket. An email at 3:14 AM gets lost among forty others and you read it Thursday. If it doesn't interrupt you, it's not an alert: it's a report someone would have to go dig up, and that someone never does.

The daily heartbeat, even though it looks like useless noise. Without it, not receiving alerts means two things at once — all fine, or all dead — and from the outside they're identical. The day the alert system itself goes down, the silence will feel reassuring for nine days.

Sounding the alarm on purpose. The most common failure isn't the flow breaking: it's the alert breaking, and that only gets discovered by triggering it. Rocío had the chat ID mistyped. She'd have known in a three-minute test, instead of during a Saturday rescue and $400 in shipping.
ignore: Serious monitoring tools: Sentry, Datadog, Grafana, Better Stack. They're built for teams with forty services and cost $30 to $90 a month. A spreadsheet tab and a Telegram bot cover you perfectly for the first several years. Come back to this once you have more than ten flows and it's hard to tell which one went down.

Staggered retries: wait a minute, then five, then twenty-five. Great idea that solves a problem you don't have yet. For now, you press the retry with your own finger, after reading the alert and understanding what happened.

Moving the log to a real database. A Google Sheets tab holds up to tens of thousands of rows. Your business partner can see it with nothing installed, and you can open it from your phone on the train. The day you notice it's getting slow, that's the day you move it, not before.
canDo: List your flow's failure modes if you describe the boxes with their real names. It'll pull out ten or fifteen, including the boring ones nobody thinks of. For example: the sheet getting renamed, a revoked permission, text arriving with a line break inside.

Write you the exact validation rules for each field, including those symbol-heavy lines that validate an email or a US phone number. And explain them in plain English, with examples that pass and examples that don't.
Draft the alert message and the what-to-do-when-it-sounds cheat sheet, with whatever length and tone you ask for. It's what it does best, and exactly what's most tedious to write by hand.

Read twenty rows of your log pasted into the chat and spot the pattern. For example: that the six failures all come from the same form. Or that they all happen between three and four in the morning, when the destination service does its maintenance.
cantDo: Know whether the alert reached your phone. It can't see your Telegram, your inbox, or your screen. A flow being well-built and an alarm actually sounding are two different things. And only one person checks the second one: you.

Test your flow for you. It doesn't have your passwords and doesn't log into your accounts, and that's good news. It can write you the four poisoned inputs, but you're the one who sends them and checks whether what was supposed to happen did.

Know what's normal for your business. A $480 order is extremely unusual for a coffee shop and totally routine for a motorcycle repair shop. You're the one who sets the ranges. If you don't, it makes them up and sets a limit that rejects good customers.

Guess which of your data is sensitive. If you don't tell it the "notes" column sometimes carries allergies or client incidents, it won't know. And it'll happily copy it into a notebook the whole team can see.
words: Validate
Checking that a piece of data has what it needs before using it: that it's there, that it isn't empty, and that it looks like what you expected. Done at the very start, not at the end.
Error branch
A box's second output, the one used only when that box fails. That's where you send the alert and the log line, instead of letting everything stop silently.
Log
A list where what your automation did every time it ran gets written down. Line by line: when, with what, and whether it went well or badly. A spreadsheet tab works fine.
Heartbeat
A short message that reaches you every day even when nothing bad happened, just to tell you the thing is still alive. The day it doesn't arrive, you know to check.
Execution
One complete run of your automation, from something coming in to it finishing. Each order triggers one. They come numbered and you can open them to see what happened inside.
Retry
Rerunning the run that failed, to see if it works this time. Great when the failure was temporary and terrible when repeating it duplicates something, like a charge or an email to a client.
Idempotent
Doing it twice leaves things the same as doing it once. Turning off a light is; charging $34.90 isn't. Before setting up automatic retries, check which case you're in.
Timeout
The maximum time your flow waits for a response before giving up on it. With no timeout, a run can hang for hours while you think everything's fine.
Review queue
A separate place, usually another sheet tab, where you park whatever failed the check so you can look at it by hand. Nothing gets thrown away, it gets set aside.
Sensitive data
Information about a person that hurts them if it leaks: their phone, their address, their card, their allergies. Never copy it into a notebook the whole team can see.
